# Apple Human Interface Guidelines

Use the relevant Apple guidance to make concrete design decisions. This package
contains a router, 13 family routes, 158 operational topic skills, and supporting
article-level references. It is
independent of Apple. The sources are a dated English HIG snapshot; check the
official source when a task depends on a newer release or a disputed detail.

## Route the task

1. Identify the target platform, device context, and user task from the request or
   project. Ask for the platform only when it materially affects the answer and
   cannot be inferred. Preserve the user's framework and product requirements.
2. Select the relevant family below and read that family's `SKILL.md`. Follow its
   link to the exact topic procedure under `.topics/` and read that `SKILL.md`.
   Apply its decision procedure, then consult its supporting article for facts
   and platform qualifications. Topic skills are explicitly read by installed
   file path; automatic nested discovery is not required.
   For platform support, product feasibility, or platform adaptation, first read each relevant
   platform's Getting started procedure, then the specific component or technology
   procedure. Check both the platform model and the surface's support limits.
3. Before finalizing the route, search the [complete topic index](references/topic-index.md)
   for the task's concepts as well as component or framework names. Its trigger
   descriptions connect everyday product requests to Apple's topic names; users
   need not name an Apple framework. Read the owning family and matching topic
   procedure before its supporting reference. Search relevant rows instead of
   loading the full corpus for a narrow question.
   For a screenshot-specific or animated example, also consult its
   [original visual explanation](references/media/index.md) when available.
4. Apply shared guidance and the target platform's documented differences. A
   missing platform subsection means no additional rule is stated; it does not
   prove support, nonapplicability, or identical behavior across platforms.
5. Compose families when the task crosses them: a component can also require
   accessibility, typography, localization, input, or system-experience guidance.
   Map the brief's material decisions to their owning topics. Read the owning
   procedure for each explicit concern, such as privacy or accessibility, as well
   as the affected components; a neighboring procedure's reminder is insufficient.
   Use [platform and task routes](references/platforms-and-tasks.md) when useful.
   In a review, map each supplied control to its candidate component procedure
   even when markup or behavior is missing. Use it to frame inspection questions;
   missing evidence neither proves a defect nor removes that control from scope.

All paths are relative to **this installed package**, not the shell's current
directory. No Python, network, sibling skill installation, or authoring cache is
required to read the guidance.

## Perform the requested work

Inspect the supplied brief, flow, code, specification or image before deciding
what is wrong or choosing a framework. Use the user's requested mode:

- **Design:** produce an implementable specification or interaction/state model
  from the topic's decision procedure, with concrete transitions and acceptance
  checks. Connect choices to the user's task and target platform.
- **Implement:** prefer the project's native system components when they supply
  the needed behavior. HIG explains experience requirements; verify API names,
  availability, and code against the appropriate SDK documentation. Make the
  authorized changes in the existing stack; a prose explanation alone does not
  complete an implementation request.
- **Review:** describe the observed problem, its effect, the relevant HIG rule,
  and a concrete correction. Separate source-backed findings from your own
  suggested improvements. Do not invent violations without inspecting evidence.
- **Adapt:** preserve the product task, data and useful state while applying the
  destination platform's interaction model. Patch the supplied artifact or give
  an explicit before/after contract when a design specification is requested.

Topic procedures are framework agnostic. Their worked examples and pseudocode
teach decisions, not a requirement to replace the project's technology. Load
related procedures only for a decision that actually depends on them.

Complete the topic's observable checks and report passed, failed and not executed
separately. Reading a file, citing Apple, or proposing a test does not establish
runtime behavior. Static code or screenshots cannot prove assistive-technology
order, native rendering, physical comfort, haptics, or SDK compilation.

Include official article/section links for material recommendations. Preserve
qualifications such as “consider,” “prefer,” and “avoid”; do not turn design
advice into invented universal requirements. Retain units and platform scope for
numerical specifications. If source passages conflict, describe the conflict
and the conservative application rather than silently changing the source.

## Source boundaries

This is comprehensive local guidance, not a verbatim Apple manual or an SDK API
reference. Original media explanations are supplementary to article references;
the source page remains useful for visual demonstrations. Source snapshots and
review status live in the repository's coverage report, outside ordinary skill
loading. Do not infer that a source has been independently reviewed just because
its local file exists.

Historical `navigation-bars` links now resolve to current Toolbars guidance;

current rules. Translations, archived pages, and complete linked SDK/WWDC libraries

# Apple HIG: Platform and task adaptation

Use this family to select and compose topic procedures. Infer the platform and
requested work from the supplied project; preserve its framework and constraints.

## Work through the decision

1. Identify the person’s primary task and the target platform before translating a screen. Read that platform’s procedure; use Principles to resolve hierarchy and Designing for games only for gameplay.
2. Compare navigation, window/scene model, primary input, attention duration and state restoration. Preserve the product task while changing the interaction appropriate to the destination platform.
3. For device changes such as opening an iPhone Duo or resizing an iPad window, specify what selection, editing state and route survive each transition.
4. Deliver a platform-decision matrix or an adaptation patch, with concrete acceptance scenarios for each materially different interaction.

inspect actual evidence and return findings; for an implementation request, make

# Apple HIG: Perception, meaning and adaptable presentation

Use this family to select and compose topic procedures. Infer the platform and
requested work from the supplied project; preserve its framework and constraints.

## Work through the decision

1. Identify the actual barrier or design decision: readability, visual hierarchy, imagery meaning, movement, locale, privacy or spatial placement. Choose the corresponding topic procedure rather than loading every foundation.
2. For text access, combine Typography with Accessibility only where size, reflow or reading alternatives matter. Use VoiceOver when grouping, semantics or navigation needs a procedure of its own.
3. For color/material decisions, separate content hierarchy from controls and evaluate the actual appearance/background/settings context. Preserve semantic meaning when appearance changes.
4. Deliver prioritized evidence-backed corrections or a concrete presentation specification. Distinguish inspected contrast/layout evidence from runtime and assistive-technology checks still needed.

# Use the iPad canvas without assuming exclusive space

Read [Designing for iPadOS](../../references/designing-for-ipados.md). Inspect the task, related content, current navigation, window assumptions, and supported touch/Pencil/keyboard/pointer paths. Identify whether people hold the iPad or work at a stand/table. Establish design, review, or adaptation mode and revise only the authorized surface using the existing stack.

Decide which relationships benefit from simultaneous visibility. Keep a list beside detail or tools beside a canvas when that reduces navigation; leave unrelated information out. Replace repeated full-screen transitions or modal panels with persistent contextual structure when space permits. At compact multitasking widths, collapse that structure while retaining selection, draft, and the route back to context.

Map each meaningful operation to the inputs the task supports. Touch remains usable without attached accessories. Precise pointer selection and keyboard commands can accelerate work; Pencil may create or annotate content without becoming a required substitute for ordinary controls. Let input methods change during the same task without discarding state or hiding essential commands behind hover.

For cross-app work, specify what can be dragged out/in and where imported content lands. Treat resizing, orientation, larger text, and another app's presence as normal operating conditions. If the iPad experience runs on Mac, identify the Mac adaptation work rather than claiming identical behavior is already native.

**Worked transformation:** Before, a sheet-music editor copies its phone flow: choose score, open full-screen tools, then return to the page after each change. Decision: editing needs score and tools together, but multitasking may narrow the window. After, a contextual tool column accompanies the score at regular width and becomes a dismissible panel at compact width, preserving page, selection, and undo history. Touch editing and keyboard commands reach the same operations.

Deliver a wide/narrow task flow and input mapping or corresponding implementation. Fail if shrinking loses a selected object, a pointer-only control blocks touch, or imported content silently replaces work. Use supplied evidence for findings; physical reach, Pencil response, and inter-app drag/drop remain unverified until exercised on supported devices.

Continue with [Layout](../../../apple-hig-foundations/.topics/apple-hig-layout/SKILL.md) for resizing, [Apple Pencil and Scribble](../../../apple-hig-inputs/.topics/apple-hig-apple-pencil-and-scribble/SKILL.md) for drawing/writing, or [Pointing devices](../../../apple-hig-inputs/.topics/apple-hig-pointing-devices/SKILL.md) for precision input.

# Designing for iPadOS Source: [Apple Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/designing-for-ipados) · Retrieved 2026-10-25. This is original application guidance based on the source text. Independent media review is recorded separately in the coverage report. iPad supports portable entertainment, detailed work, and creative activity. Its large high-resolution display may be held, placed on a table, or used on a stand; typical viewing distance stays within about 3 feet. ## Best practices - Elevate useful content with the larger canvas. Reduce modal interruptions and full-screen transitions; keep controls reachable without obscuring the work. - Choose content density and sizing for both viewing distance and current input method. - Support combinations of touch, onscreen keyboard, attached keyboard, mouse or trackpad, Apple Pencil, and voice. Mixed-input workflows are normal. - Expect both quick actions and hours-long sessions. Support several visible apps, multitasking, and inter-app drag and drop rather than assuming exclusive use of the display. - Adapt continuously to orientation, multitasking sizes, Dark Mode, and Dynamic Type. Preserve a coherent experience when the iPad app runs on macOS. - Consider widgets, multitasking support, and drag and drop as integrated parts of the experience. ## Resources Consult the [official article](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/designing-for-ipados) for linked Apple design assets and implementation resources. #### Related The official article links the adjacent HIG topics relevant to this guidance. #### Developer documentation Use the framework references linked by Apple for current API availability and implementation details. #### Videos Apple’s linked design sessions provide demonstrations and additional implementation context; no video review is implied here.

# Preserve relationships while available space changes

Read [Layout](../../references/layout.md). Inspect content priority, navigation, controls, supported environments, constraints, and current implementation. Identify design/review/adaptation mode and keep the existing layout system. Record actual available space and text/localization conditions; device names alone are insufficient evidence for a breakpoint.

Start with relationships: align peers, group related items, indent subordinates, and reveal secondary choices progressively. Place important content toward the leading/top region in the locale's reading order. Separate backgrounds that can extend beneath bars from important content/actions that must respect safe regions.

Choose adaptations from available width/height and environmental values, not a phone/tablet or portrait/landscape guess. Preserve selection, content, functionality, and idiom when columns collapse, actions overflow, or horizontal rows stack for larger text. Test the smallest and largest useful layouts first, then intermediate resizing, longer localization, direction changes, and display accommodations. Crop decorative backgrounds without distorting aspect ratio or hiding essential imagery.

Apply platform conditions deliberately: Mac essential controls cannot depend on a bottom edge that may be offscreen; TV content needs the guide's overscan insets and focus-expansion room; Watch normally needs very few side-by-side actions. visionOS windows/volumes should resize, use meaningful bounds, and avoid inline 3D crowding controls; use separate volumes for model-centric work. Read numeric platform specifications from the guide rather than generalizing one platform's spacing.

**Before → decision → after:** A reading list positions Delete at a fixed bottom coordinate and fixes each row to one line. Decision: resized windows and enlarged titles need flow-based layout. After, row height/wrapping adapt, secondary actions remain reachable through contextual overflow, and the selected article persists when the sidebar collapses.

Deliver corrected layouts/constraints or implementation plus an environment matrix. Fail if a required action disappears, related items detach, content overlaps hardware/bars, or resizing changes the task's meaning. Report tested dimensions/settings; static or Linux checks cannot establish native safe-area/focus behavior absent supported execution.

Use [Typography](../apple-hig-typography/SKILL.md) for text behavior, [Right to left](../apple-hig-right-to-left/SKILL.md) for direction, and [Spatial layout](../apple-hig-spatial-layout/SKILL.md) for 3D position/scale.

# Mirror meaning rather than every pixel

Preserve the existing framework's directional behavior before adding manual overrides; mark locale-specific assumptions requiring native-language review.

Classify each directional element. Reading-order navigation, progress controls, endpoint labels, and meaningful ordered image collections generally reverse position/direction. Literal physical directions or controls aimed at a specific onscreen place retain that meaning. Preserve photographs, logos, universal signs, and ordinary object/tool handedness; localize strongly directional art rather than blindly flipping it.

Handle text at the right level. Short labels follow interface alignment; longer paragraphs follow their own language, including mixed-language content. Keep list alignment consistent even when one entry uses another script. Preserve digit order in numbers, phones, and card numbers while adapting locale-specific numeral/currency formatting and the position of ordered sequences.

Use directional/localized SF Symbol variants. Review a custom complex glyph component by component: its base, badge position, actual text, and negation slash can have different needs. If Latin uppercase neighbors Arabic/Hebrew labels, evaluate optical balance rather than assuming equal numeric point size looks equal. Hardware-linked controls retain any platform-specific physical placement instead of inheriting a generic mirror rule.

**Worked transformation:** Before, an Arabic cycling app flips the map photo, bicycle glyph, phone digits, and Back arrow together. Decision: only reading-order navigation should mirror; the other elements describe real content or fixed sequences. After, Back and progress order adapt, the map/photo and bicycle handedness remain correct, and phone digits retain their internal order under localized formatting.

Deliver a corrected directional screen/asset mapping or implementation. Fail if reading-order navigation points the wrong way, digits reverse internally, real artwork changes meaning, or a mixed-language paragraph follows the wrong alignment. # Preserve readable hierarchy as text grows

Read [Typography](../../references/typography.md). Inspect the actual text roles, font files/styles, platform, viewing context, and resizing behavior. Establish design, review, or adaptation mode. Use the guide's platform style/size tables when exact values matter; do not reproduce the entire specification or confuse its minimum with a comfortable default.

Assign semantic roles before choosing sizes: title, body, supporting detail, and actionable label need a clear relationship. Prefer system text styles and runtime font APIs so optical design/tracking adapt to size. If a custom face is needed, verify weight/legibility and provide equivalent text-size and Bold Text behavior; thin faces may need more size than the table suggests. Use loose leading for sustained/wide reading, avoiding tight leading across three or more lines.

Decide how content expands. Grow containers, permit labels to wrap, stack timestamps/glyphs, and reduce columns rather than aggressively truncating essential reading. Scale meaningful glyphs with the text. Preserve hierarchy while prioritizing the content people intend to read; not every decorative/transient number must grow identically.

On visionOS, favor readable 2D text, explicit styles for New York, little extrusion, and viewer-facing object labels; do not rely on cast shadows against unpredictable surroundings. Watch uses its own font conventions, including complication typography.

After, titles use a legible role/weight, wrap into growing rows, supporting text stacks, and meaningful glyphs scale while selection/actions stay available.

# Make the task accessible

Read [Accessibility guidance](../../references/accessibility.md) before applying platform values. This procedure turns that guidance into task-level changes; its artifact format and prioritization are application engineering advice, not additional Apple requirements.

## Establish what can be evaluated

Identify the supported platform, the person's task from entry to completion, and whether the request is design, review, or adaptation. Inspect the supplied screens, content, interaction description, semantics, or implementation. Record which evidence exists: a screenshot can establish visible labels and geometry, but cannot establish spoken names, focus order, alternative activation, or preference behavior. Continue using explicit assumptions when the platform or behavior is missing; ask only when the choice changes the requested result.

For a review, connect each finding to an observed barrier and its consequence for that task. Separate untested behavior needing verification from confirmed defects. For a design or adaptation, change the authorized artifact itself: a revised screen specification, interaction contract, or implementation. A general accessibility checklist alone is not the deliverable.

## Remove the barriers that the task contains

Trace the task without assuming sight, hearing, fine motor control, speech, or fast responses. Select the applicable branches:

- **Reading and visual distinctions:** Preserve content and available actions when text enlarges. Use the guide's platform-specific text defaults and minima; its resizing guidance is at least 200%, with 140% stated for watchOS. Reflow or expose another usable arrangement rather than clipping essential labels. Pair color distinctions with text, shape, or symbols. Evaluate actual foreground/background combinations in light and dark appearances; use a contrast calculator and preserve the guide's stated contrast-table scope instead of claiming that its values alone establish conformance. If the default scheme falls short, specify the Increase Contrast treatment.
- **Information carried by sound or imagery:** Identify what information would disappear when sound or sight is unavailable. Choose captions for synchronized audible events, subtitles for dialogue translation, audio description for visual events, or transcripts for a complete text account according to the content. Specify descriptions for meaningful interface/content imagery and omit redundant decoration. Pair essential sound feedback with a perceivable visual or appropriate haptic equivalent.
- **Manipulation and navigation:** Distinguish visible control size from its actual activation area and separation. Use the guide's platform default as the starting point; its smaller minimum is not a blanket recommendation for dense controls. Replace essential complex or repeated gestures with a labeled onscreen action. Make the complete task navigable and activatable with the supported keyboard and assistive input paths; speech must not be necessary. Preserve system accessibility shortcuts. For custom controls, specify names, roles, values, states, and task order rather than assuming their appearance supplies semantics.
- **Time, motion, and comprehension:** Give people time to read and act; prefer explicit dismissal when transient content requires attention. If motion is present, define a Reduce Motion version that retains state and meaning while reducing automatic movement, bounce, zoom, or depth changes. If media autoplays, provide playback control and consider a global preference; honor Dim Flashing Lights where applicable. Keep the task's navigation and wording consistent rather than adding instructional clutter.

Apply the relevant platform condition. For Assistive Access on iOS/iPadOS, focus on core tasks with one interaction per screen and the source's two confirmations for difficult-to-reverse actions in that mode. For visionOS, keep controls in comfortable view, avoid head-locked content and repeated large gestures, and accommodate hand/head Pointer Control and Zoom. These conditions do not apply automatically to every platform.

## Deliver and check the result

Return the revised artifact or evidence-based review, including the barrier, the concrete change, and its acceptance check. State which platform/preferences were considered and which claims remain unverified. Prioritize blockers to completing the task over cosmetic refinements.

Exercise each selected alternative along the same entry-to-completion path. Fail the check if essential content or actions disappear at the specified text scale, information remains available through only one sense, a required gesture has no equivalent, focus cannot reach/activate a necessary control, or a requested motion accommodation removes meaning. Measure contrast and activation geometry when the evidence permits; report missing measurements rather than inventing them. Use Accessibility Inspector and relevant VoiceOver, Switch Control, Full Keyboard Access, AssistiveTouch, or Pointer Control tests on supported Apple environments. Static inspection or a Linux run cannot establish those runtime results, Apple-device comfort, or App Store Accessibility Nutrition Label eligibility.

## Worked transformation

**Before:** An iPad astronomy log marks observation quality only with green/red dots, announces saving with a chime, and exposes Delete only by a two-finger gesture.

**Decision:** Logging must remain understandable without color or sound and operable without that gesture. Retain compact rows while making status and actions explicit.

**After:** Each row reads “Clear” or “Clouded” alongside its symbol; saving exposes a persistent “Saved” state; a labeled row action opens Delete. The screen specification includes expanded-text reflow, semantic row status, and keyboard/assistive activation acceptance checks. These are proposed changes until the actual implementation passes those checks; the specification does not claim VoiceOver was tested.

## Continue only where needed

For detailed spoken structure and rotor navigation, use [VoiceOver](../../../apple-hig-technologies/.topics/apple-hig-voiceover/SKILL.md). For text reflow/type choices use [Typography](../apple-hig-typography/SKILL.md); for a motion accommodation use [Motion](../apple-hig-motion/SKILL.md). # Make commands discoverable and preserve familiar keys

Read [Keyboards](../../references/keyboards.md). Inspect task commands, text-entry contexts, current bindings, supported platforms/locales, and requested design/review/adaptation. Physical keyboards are covered on every listed platform except watchOS. Preserve the existing stack and identify actual keyboard evidence before claiming complete navigation.

Reuse familiar standard shortcuts for their expected meanings; consult the guide's mapping in context rather than treating legacy/system entries as universally available app APIs. # Operate on buttons

Read [the buttons guide](../../references/buttons.md) before making HIG claims. This procedure is application advice for turning that guide into an artifact; platform facts and dimensions come from the guide. Preserve the user's framework and authorized scope.

## Establish the action contract

Inspect the supplied screen, code, prototype, or brief. Identify the target platform, input methods, surrounding task, and requested mode: create, review, or adapt. For each consequential button, record its visible label or symbol, activation outcome, affected object, reversibility, current role/default status, and actual hit region if available. A screenshot can establish visible styling; it cannot establish hit geometry, keyboard behavior, or accessible names. Mark those as unknown and inspect implementation when available.

Classify the action before styling it. An immediate command fits a button. A persistent on/off setting may need a toggle; choosing one of several persistent options may need a segmented control or picker; a menu-opening control needs the corresponding menu button behavior. Retain a button when its action is to open that choice, but distinguish opening from committing a choice.

## Make and apply the consequential choices

1. Write an outcome-specific short verb phrase, or use a familiar symbol whose meaning survives its context. Give an icon-only control an accessible name that states the action. Do not assume a tooltip replaces the name. On Mac, an ellipsis indicates that another window, view, or app requires further input; add it based on the continuation, not merely because an operation takes time.
2. Assign semantic roles from consequences. Prefer one or two prominent likely actions per view and use style rather than unequal sizes to rank related choices. A primary/default action should normally be the likely nondestructive choice. If destruction is involved, consult the alerts topic before deciding confirmation and Return behavior: the guide explicitly allows a deliberate-destruction alert exception, so “destructive can never be default” is not a universal rule. Cancel abandons the current task; it is not a generic label for completing it.
3. Choose the system control/style when available, retaining its states and accessibility behavior. For a custom control, specify perceivable press feedback and preserve meaningful focus, enabled/disabled, and selected states as applicable. State the reason for a disabled action when the surrounding context does not explain it. This is application advice, not a new Apple requirement to add all states to every button.
4. Check visual and selectable geometry separately. Apply the guide's target and separation rules for the actual platform; a small glyph or small visual style does not establish a small hit region. On visionOS, retain a discernible shape/fill, use standard audible/state feedback, and inspect center spacing and hover overlap. Do not propose unsupported custom hover effects or haptics there. On watchOS, choose inline versus toolbar placement deliberately; preserve common heights for peer controls and use short labels for side-by-side actions. On Mac, distinguish view-body square/image/help buttons from toolbar items; apply the help-button placement/count rules only when designing Help.
5. Only when the command has delayed completion, define the initiating, waiting, and resolved behavior. On iOS/iPadOS, use the activating button's activity indication as described in the guide, preserving context and replacing its image when appropriate. Specify how duplicate activation is handled and what success or failure means in the product; do not promise network completion from a press animation.

Perform the authorized work: implement the controls in the supplied project for a build request; produce an annotated control specification for a design request; or report evidence-backed defects and exact corrections for a review. For adaptation, map each affected control to its destination platform rather than copying appearance alone.

## Deliver and verify

Return the changed artifact or a compact button contract containing label/name, outcome, role/default, style/placement, target region, and relevant state behavior. In review mode attach findings to identifiable controls and separate observed defects from checks requiring execution.

Verify that activation reaches the named outcome; cancellation leaves the intended prior state; keyboard/default activation cannot commit an unintended outcome; focus and accessible names identify the action; and enlarged labels do not clip or overlap adjacent targets. Measure hit regions from layout/runtime data when available. Fail the design if a destructive consequence is mislabeled, peer targets overlap, an icon has no discoverable name, or custom press feedback is absent. State separately which checks were inspected in source, exercised, or remain Apple-device checks; Linux inspection does not prove gaze, VoiceOver, haptics, or native rendering.

## Worked transformation

**Before:** A Mac photo organizer has equally prominent `Go`, `Remove`, and `Close` buttons. `Go` opens export settings; `Remove` deletes a selection with undo; `Close` finishes editing metadata.

**Decision:** The labels hide three different contracts. Export requires further input; routine reversible removal does not by itself justify a confirmation alert; finishing edits should name completion. The export task, rather than removal, is the likely action on this screen.

**After:** Specify `Export…` as the prominent action opening export settings, `Remove Photos` as a lower-emphasis command with a visible Undo path, and `Done` for finishing metadata edits. Inspect actual save semantics before changing `Close` to `Done`. Verify the Return mapping, undo restoration, and that each accessible name matches the resulting action. These product choices are an example application, not facts about the unseen implementation.

## Conditional handoffs

Load alerts for consequential confirmation/default decisions; toggles or segmented-controls for persistent selection; pop-up-buttons or pull-down-buttons for menu-opening behavior; toolbars when placement belongs to window chrome; and accessibility when naming, focus, contrast, or target access needs deeper work. Keep this button contract as the input to the next topic.

# Layout Source: [Apple Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/layout) · Retrieved 2026-10-25. This is original application guidance based on the source text. Independent media review is recorded separately in the coverage report. Use predictable relationships among content and controls while adapting to the actual available space. ## Visual hierarchy Prioritize important content toward the top and leading edge in reading order. Use system components for RTL adaptation. Align related items, indent subordinate items, and group relationships with space, containers, or separators. Reveal secondary choices progressively through disclosure, menus, nested views, or scrollable media sections. Distinguish navigation/controls with Liquid Glass and scroll-edge treatments; extend full-window backgrounds under bars and sidebars. A background extension effect can mirror and blur imagery under adjacent components instead of hiding essential original art. ## Adaptability Handle size classes, display sizes, orientation/aspect ratio, Dynamic Island, external displays, Display Zoom, resizable windows, text changes, localized length/direction/fonts, and date/number formats. Use SwiftUI or Auto Layout, safe areas, margins, and layout modifiers. Orientation-locked games must still resize. With large text, stack horizontal content, increase row height, and allow wrapping. Apple’s Unity accessibility plug-in can supply Dynamic Type in games. Preview smallest/largest layouts first, then multiple devices, localizations, sizes, iPad resizing, and iPhone Mirroring. Scale backgrounds to fill without distorting aspect ratio; extreme wide/short or narrow/tall windows may crop much more than standard displays. ### Size classes Each axis is compact or regular, describing available width or height rather than device type or orientation. All four combinations can occur as apps resize, multitask, or mirror. Base layout on these environmental values, not idiom/orientation guesses. Preserve functionality across classes while changing how much is exposed, such as sidebar versus tabs or visible actions versus overflow. The platform idiom remains the same during resizing, so preserve its familiar character. ## Guides and safe areas Layout guides supply rectangular regions for alignment, spacing, margins, and readable text widths; custom guides can add app-specific structure. Safe areas exclude edge obstructions such as camera hardware, status bars, tab bars, and toolbars. Keep important content and controls within the appropriate safe regions. ## Platform considerations No extra iOS/iPadOS rules are listed. ### macOS Do not rely on the bottom of a window for essential controls because it may sit below the physical display. Avoid placing content behind the top camera housing. ### tvOS Inset primary content 60 pt vertically and 80 pt horizontally to withstand TV overscan/settings. Leave enough focus padding for system enlargement so focused items do not obscure important information. #### Grids Use consistent row/column spacing, sufficient room for enlargement, and symmetrical partial items at both horizontal edges. Add extra separation above and below row titles. UIKit collection flow layout derives the column count from item width and spacing. Source grid measurements follow; all use 40 pt horizontal gaps and a minimum 100 pt vertical gap between unfocused rows. #### Two-column grid Unfocused item width: 860 pt. Horizontal gap: 40 pt. Minimum vertical gap: 100 pt. #### Three-column grid Unfocused item width: 560 pt. Horizontal gap: 40 pt. Minimum vertical gap: 100 pt. #### Four-column grid Unfocused item width: 410 pt. Horizontal gap: 40 pt. Minimum vertical gap: 100 pt. #### Five-column grid Unfocused item width: 320 pt. Horizontal gap: 40 pt. Minimum vertical gap: 100 pt. #### Six-column grid Unfocused item width: 260 pt. Horizontal gap: 40 pt. Minimum vertical gap: 100 pt. #### Seven-column grid Unfocused item width: 217 pt. Horizontal gap: 40 pt. Minimum vertical gap: 100 pt. #### Eight-column grid Unfocused item width: 184 pt. Horizontal gap: 40 pt. Minimum vertical gap: 100 pt. #### Nine-column grid Unfocused item width: 160 pt. Horizontal gap: 40 pt. Minimum vertical gap: 100 pt. ### visionOS Support resizing in windows and volumes; center content horizontally at very large sizes. Set minimum/maximum bounds only to avoid overlaps or unwieldy layouts, not to disable resizing. Use inline 3D content sparingly for meaningful additions; inset it so it avoids controls and window edges. Prefer volumes or immersive spaces for large/model-centric content. Open supplemental content in an adjacent window, reserving ornaments for interactive app controls. Space controls so hover feedback remains distinct; regular buttons should have centers at least 60 pt apart. ### watchOS Normally use no more than three glyph buttons or two text buttons side by side. Use standard framework layout so RTL languages such as Arabic and Hebrew adapt naturally. Fine-tune direction, localized numbers/currency/math, and custom assets where system behavior is insufficient. ## Text alignment Mirror short labels and one/two-line blocks with the interface. Align paragraphs of three or more lines according to the paragraph’s own language, which can differ from the surrounding UI. This is original application guidance based on the source text. Independent media review is recorded separately in the coverage report. ## Contents - [Ensuring legibility](#Ensuring-legibility) - [Conveying hierarchy](#Conveying-hierarchy) - [Using system fonts](#Using-system-fonts) - [Using custom fonts](#Using-custom-fonts) - [Supporting Dynamic Type](#Supporting-Dynamic-Type) - [Platform considerations](#Platform-considerations) - [Specifications](#Specifications) - [Resources](#Resources) - [Change log](#Change-log) ## Ensuring legibility Test type at real viewing distances, lighting conditions, and supported devices. Enlarge hard-to-read text, improve foreground/background contrast, or choose a more legible face. Prefer Regular, Medium, Semibold, or Bold over Ultralight/Thin/Light, especially at small sizes. Thin custom faces often need sizes above the recommendations. |Platform|Default|Minimum| |---|---:|---:| |iOS, iPadOS|17 pt|11 pt| |macOS|13 pt|10 pt| |tvOS|29 pt|23 pt| |visionOS|17 pt|12 pt| |watchOS|16 pt|12 pt| ## Conveying hierarchy Combine size, weight, and color to distinguish levels, and preserve those relationships as text grows. Limit typeface families so differences retain meaning. Prioritize content people intend to read when scaling: body/dialogue may need growth while tab labels or transient damage numbers need not grow equally. ## Using system fonts San Francisco includes Pro, Compact, Arabic, Armenian, Georgian, Hebrew, and Mono variants; all listed except Mono also have rounded alternatives. New York is a complementary serif family. Variable fonts interpolate weights and optical design continuously for the exact point size, rather than requiring separate Text/Display font choices except in limited design tools. SF offers widths such as Condensed/Expanded and weights from Ultralight through Black; equivalent SF Symbol weights enable precise matching. Use semantic text styles to express hierarchy through coordinated weight, size, and leading, and to inherit Dynamic Type/accessibility adjustments where supported. Modify symbolic traits for emphasis or line spacing when justified. Loose leading supports long passages or wide columns; tight leading can fit constrained rows, but avoid it for three or more lines. Access system fonts through platform APIs (`default`, `serif`, and the font-design constants), without embedding the files. Runtime tracking adapts by size automatically; mockups may need the tracking values below. ## Using custom fonts Check custom faces against platform size recommendations and actual conditions. Implement Dynamic Type and Bold Text behavior equivalent to the system faces. Apple’s Unity accessibility plug-in can support Dynamic Type in games; if unsuitable, offer a separate text-size adjustment. ## Supporting Dynamic Type Dynamic Type is available in iOS, iPadOS, tvOS, visionOS, and watchOS. Test every supported size, including Larger Accessibility Text on iPhone/iPad. Scale meaningful glyphs as well as text; SF Symbols integrate automatically. Preserve useful information at the largest accessibility size rather than aggressively truncating. Give labels enough lines and avoid truncation in scrolling regions unless a detail view exposes the full text. Stack inline timestamps/glyphs beneath or above primary text, grow containers, and reduce columns when width becomes cramped. Keep important content toward the top and the overall hierarchy stable. ## Platform considerations ### iOS, iPadOS SF Pro is standard; New York is also available. ### macOS SF Pro is standard and New York is available to Mac Catalyst apps. macOS has no Dynamic Type. Match standard-control typography with the relevant NSFont methods: `controlContentFont`, `labelFont`, `menuFont`, `menuBarFont`, `messageFont`, `paletteFont`, `titleBarFont`, `toolTipsFont`, `userFont`, `userFixedPitchFont`, `boldSystemFont`, and `systemFont`, each with its `ofSize:` parameter. ### tvOS SF Pro is standard, with New York also available. ### visionOS SF Pro is standard; specify text styles explicitly when using New York. Body/title Dynamic Type styles are bolder, and Extra Large Title 1/2 support wide editorial compositions. Prefer readable 2D text with little or no extrusion. Test full-scale designs through different viewing scales. Default white text contrasts with glass; test custom colors against diverse surroundings. Without a container background, bold can improve visibility; do not rely on unpredictable cast shadows. Billboard labels associated with 3D objects toward the viewer, normally rotating around the y-axis so the baseline stays perpendicular to the line of sight. ### watchOS SF Compact is standard, New York is available, and complications use SF Compact Rounded. ## Specifications Values below preserve the source’s factual measurements. # Accessibility Source: [Apple Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/accessibility) · Retrieved 2026-10-25. This is original application guidance based on the source text. Independent media review is recorded separately in the coverage report. Build an interface people can understand, perceive through different senses, and adapt to their preferred methods. Treat accessibility as a design input and audit with Accessibility Inspector. Evaluate actual support before describing Accessibility Nutrition Labels on the App Store. ## Vision Support text enlargement of at least 200%; the source gives 140% for watchOS. Dynamic Type or equivalent custom resizing must preserve usability. Follow platform defaults/minima when choosing custom styles, and enlarge thin-weight custom fonts further when needed. |Platform|Default text|Minimum text| |---|---:|---:| |iOS, iPadOS|17 pt|11 pt| |macOS|13 pt|10 pt| |tvOS|29 pt|23 pt| |visionOS|17 pt|12 pt| |watchOS|16 pt|12 pt| Measure contrast using established calculators such as WCAG or APCA. Apple’s Accessibility Inspector table uses these WCAG-AA guidance values: text up to 17 pt, all weights, 4.5:1; 18 pt at all weights, 3:1; bold text at any size, 3:1. Preserve the table’s stated scope rather than assuming it replaces a separate conformance evaluation. If default colors fall short, Increase Contrast must supply a higher-contrast scheme. Test both light and dark. Prefer semantic system colors that adapt to accessibility preferences. Pair color with shape, icons, or text; red/green and blue/orange distinctions can be difficult. Let people customize chart or character colors where useful. Give VoiceOver meaningful descriptions of interface and content. ## Hearing Make dialogue and important information available without sound. Captions describe audible information in synchrony with media, subtitles present dialogue in a chosen language, audio descriptions narrate otherwise visual events in audio pauses, and transcripts provide a complete text account of audible and visual information. Let people adjust text presentation. Pair sound feedback with matching haptics and visual direction cues, especially for offscreen game or spatial events. Music Haptics and audio graphs on iOS/iPadOS can offer tactile representations of music and data. ## Mobility Use comfortable controls and sufficient separation, not just adequate visible size. |Platform|Default control|Minimum control| |---|---:|---:| |iOS, iPadOS|44 × 44 pt|28 × 28 pt| |macOS|28 × 28 pt|20 × 20 pt| |tvOS|66 × 66 pt|56 × 56 pt| |visionOS|60 × 60 pt|28 × 28 pt| |watchOS|44 × 44 pt|28 × 28 pt| The source suggests around 12 pt padding for bezelled elements and 24 pt outside visible edges for elements without a bezel. Use simple gestures for repeated tasks and offer an onscreen alternative for essential gestures, such as a dismiss button alongside swipe-to-dismiss. Avoid requiring complex multiple-finger or multiple-hand actions. Label controls so Voice Control can target them. Siri/Shortcuts can expose repeated tasks through voice, Action buttons, Home Screen, and Control Center. Test VoiceOver, AssistiveTouch, Full Keyboard Access, Pointer Control, and Switch Control rather than assuming support. ## Speech Support complete keyboard navigation and Full Keyboard Access; preserve system accessibility shortcuts. Support Switch Control navigation and activation through hardware, controller, and sound inputs such as a click or pop, so speech is never a necessary input method. ## Cognitive Use familiar, simple, consistent navigation and gestures. Prefer explicit dismissal over timed disappearance, allowing time for processing and assistive navigation. Games can offer difficulty, reaction-time, success-criteria, and control-assistance accommodations. Give clear playback controls and consider a global autoplay preference. Respect Dim Flashing Lights during media playback. Honor Reduce Motion by reducing automatic and repeated movement, scaling, zooming, and peripheral effects. Reduce spring bounce; tie appropriate motion directly to gestures; avoid animated depth changes and blur transitions; replace spatial translations with fades. Fast or blinking motion can distract, cause dizziness, or trigger seizures. For Assistive Access on iOS/iPadOS, focus on core tasks, remove nonessential workflows, and split multistep tasks into one interaction per screen. The source requires two confirmations for actions that are difficult to reverse, such as deletion, in this mode. ## Platform considerations The source adds no separate rules for iOS, iPadOS, macOS, tvOS, or watchOS beyond the guidance above. ### visionOS Support hand/head Pointer Control and Zoom. Keep controls inside a comfortable field of view; horizontal arrangements usually strain the neck less than tall ones. Avoid rapid shifts of attention among distant locations. Reduce peripheral animation speed and intensity, use gentle camera/video motion, and avoid making the surrounding world move without the person’s control. Do not lock content to the head, which can feel confining and interfere with Pointer Control. Minimize large or repeated gestures and consider the physical surroundings. ## Resources Consult the [official article](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/accessibility) for linked Apple design assets and implementation resources. #### Related The official article links the adjacent HIG topics relevant to this guidance. #### Developer documentation Use the framework references linked by Apple for current API availability and implementation details. #### Videos Apple’s linked design sessions provide demonstrations and additional implementation context; no video review is implied here. ## Change log Source revision dates: June 9, 2025, March 7, 2025, June 10, 2024, December 5, 2023, June 21, 2023.

# Focus and selection Source: [Apple Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/focus-and-selection) · Retrieved 2026-10-25. This is original application guidance based on the source text. Independent media review is recorded separately in the coverage report. Focus visually identifies an interaction target for component-based navigation with keyboards, remotes, and controllers. Focus can select an item automatically, except where selection would shift context; tvOS normally requires separate activation. Rings/highlights on tablet/Mac and depth/parallax on TV reflect their platform focus models. ## Best practices Use system focus effects unless customization is essential. Do not move focus without input. If a focused item disappears during discrete directional navigation, move to a nearby one-step item; with other input, hide the indicator rather than guessing the next target. Follow platform reachability conventions: keyboard content focus on iPad/Mac coexists with Full Keyboard Access for all controls, whereas tvOS requires directional access to every interactive item. Use rings for text/search and usually full-row highlights for lists/collections. Standard focused/unfocused selection colors preserve active context. ## Platform considerations The source marks focus unsupported on iOS/watchOS in this topic’s sense. ### iPadOS Since iPadOS 15, Tab moves between focus groups and arrows move inside a group. Group custom views to produce expected reading order, normally leading-to-trailing then top-to-bottom; a vertical stack may need one focus-group container. Set priority so a likely primary item receives focus when a group is entered. Halo effects outline an item and can be refined for shape, clipping, or badge overlap. A content-configured cell’s highlighted accent appearance is separate from a focus effect. ### tvOS In full-screen content, gestures should act on the content rather than invisible focus. Use component focus for menus instead of a tiny free pointer; a gameplay-specific pointer must be conspicuous and integrated. Allow room and high-resolution art for enlarged focus states. Represent unfocused (receded), focused (raised/lit/moving), pressed (immediate feedback), selected (persistent choice such as filled favorite), and unavailable (inactive and unreachable) states distinctly. ### visionOS Connected keyboards/controllers use the same focus system family. Looking at content uses hover feedback instead; do not treat gaze hover as keyboard/controller focus. ## Resources Consult the [official article](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/focus-and-selection) for linked Apple design assets and implementation resources. #### Related The official article links the adjacent HIG topics relevant to this guidance. #### Developer documentation Use the framework references linked by Apple for current API availability and implementation details. #### Videos Apple’s linked design sessions provide demonstrations and additional implementation context; no video review is implied here. ## Change log Source revision dates: October 24, 2023, June 21, 2023.

# Text fields Source: [Apple Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/text-fields) Snapshot: 2026-10-25. Original implementation guidance derived from the source. Use a text field for a short, specific value such as a name or email address. A text view is the better primitive for extended text. ## Best practices - Explain purpose with a placeholder, and add a persistent external label where losing the placeholder during entry would make the field ambiguous. - Use secure entry for sensitive content. Size fields to suggest expected input length; stack groups with even spacing and consistent widths where possible so labels remain clearly associated. - Keep Tab traversal in the expected logical order, using system behavior unless a correction is needed. - Validate at a useful moment. Email validation often belongs when leaving the field; username/password creation feedback should occur before leaving it. Reject values incompatible with the required format with understandable feedback. - Use number formatters for numeric constraints and representations such as decimal precision, percentages, and currency, retaining locale-sensitive formatting. - Choose overflow behavior intentionally: system defaults clip, but character/word wrapping or beginning/middle/end ellipses may better fit the task. An expansion tooltip can reveal full clipped content to a pointer user. - Select the appropriate virtual keyboard for iOS, iPadOS, tvOS, and visionOS. Minimize both field count and lengthy entry on tvOS and watchOS; choices or buttons can gather information more efficiently. ## Platform considerations No additional tvOS or visionOS rules are specified. ### iOS, iPadOS Offer a trailing Clear control to erase the current value in one action. Leading imagery can explain purpose; trailing buttons can offer extra functionality, such as bookmarking. ### macOS A combo box is useful when free typing should coexist with a predefined set of likely choices. ### watchOS Request typed text only when necessary; prefer selecting an existing option. ## Resources Official implementation links and revision metadata follow. #### Related [Text views](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/text-views) [Combo boxes](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/combo-boxes) [Entering data](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/entering-data) #### Developer documentation — SwiftUI — SwiftUI — UIKit — AppKit ## Change log Revision dates recorded by Apple: June 5, 2023.

# Buttons Source: [Apple Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/buttons) Snapshot: 2026-10-25. Original implementation guidance derived from the source. ## Contents - [Best practices](#Best-practices) - [Style](#Style) - [Content](#Content) - [Role](#Role) - [Platform considerations](#Platform-considerations) A button performs an immediate action. Its visual style, visible symbol/text, and semantic role work together to explain what activation does. ## Best practices Allow enough surrounding space for clear separation and easy selection. General hit regions should be at least 44×44 pt; visionOS targets need 60×60 pt. Custom buttons always need press feedback. ## Style Prefer system styles for built-in states, accessibility, and appearance adaptation. Use one or two prominent buttons per view for likely actions. Distinguish a preferred option through style rather than making related buttons different sizes. Keep label colors distinct from colorful content; the default monochrome often works best over rich backgrounds. ## Content Use a familiar symbol for a familiar action; use a short title-case verb phrase when words are clearer. Mac and visionOS can provide brief hover tooltips; text-labeled buttons usually explain themselves. ## Role Normal has no special meaning; primary is the expected/default action; Cancel abandons the current action; destructive signals data loss. Roles affect rendering, such as accent fill for primary and red for destructive. Primary can respond to Return and close a temporary view. Generally assign primary only to a nondestructive likely action. Application advice: consult the alert-specific deliberate-destruction exception before prescribing confirmation behavior. ## Platform considerations No additional tvOS rules are specified. ### iOS, iPadOS For delayed completion, show an activity indicator within the activating button, optionally changing its label to the current operation. The indicator replaces any button image while preserving context for the wait. ### macOS #### Push buttons The standard push button can show text, imagery, or both and can serve as default. Use flexible height for tall icons or multiple text lines, otherwise retain standard sizing. Append an ellipsis when the button opens another window/view/app for further input. Consider spring loading through a dragged selection plus force-click on Magic Trackpad, preserving the drag afterward. #### Square buttons These small glyph-only controls affect a nearby view, for example adding/removing table rows. They can act as push, toggle, or pop-up controls. Use them in the body rather than the frame, toolbar, or status bar. Prefer system symbols and omit introductory labels when proximity explains the function. #### Help buttons Use the familiar system question-mark control, at most one per window, opening context-specific help when possible and top-level help otherwise. In a dialog with dismissal controls, place it in the opposite lower corner, aligned vertically with those controls. Without dismissal controls, or in settings, use either lower corner. Keep it in the view body and omit explanatory introductory text. #### Image buttons Image buttons can act as push, toggle, or pop-up controls inside a view. Toolbar imagery instead belongs to a toolbar item. Allow about 10 pixels between image and clickable button edges and generally omit a visible system border. Put any needed label beneath the image. ### visionOS Buttons normally have a visible background and audible feedback. A look-triggered tooltip can explain a glyph. | Shape | Supported visual sizes | | --- | --- | | Circle | Mini 28 pt; small 32 pt; regular 44 pt; large 52 pt; extra large 64 pt | | Text capsule | Small 32 pt; regular 44 pt; large 52 pt | | Text-and-icon capsule | Regular 44 pt; large 52 pt | | Rounded rectangle | Small 32 pt; regular 44 pt; large 52 pt | Visual size does not remove the 60-pt targeting requirement. # Windows Source: [Apple Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/windows) Snapshot: 2026-10-25. Original implementation guidance derived from the source. Primary windows host app navigation, content, and actions. Auxiliary windows focus on one task or area and typically close after that task. iPadOS, macOS, and visionOS windows establish content boundaries and enable multitasking with system movement, sizing, and closing controls. ## Best practices Adapt smoothly to size changes. Open new windows when preserving context or working in parallel helps, without generating clutter by default. Offer Open in New Window in a context or File menu when useful. Retain system frames and controls instead of imitating them. Call the experience a window in user-facing copy; scene is an implementation term. ## Platform considerations This multiwindow component guidance marks iOS, tvOS, and watchOS unsupported. ### iPadOS People choose fullscreen or windowed behavior in Multitasking & Gestures settings. Fullscreen fills the display and uses app switching; windowed mode supports multiple resizable, movable windows with remembered placement. Move leading toolbar items inward when window controls appear so they do not overlap. Consider gestures to open content in a new window, such as expanding a collection item with a pinch. Quick Look can present a single file without a custom window if the app supports multiple windows. ### macOS Support normal movement, resize, minimization, and frequent switching among multiple apps' windows. Games also need the appropriate system game-window configuration. #### macOS window anatomy A frame above the body supplies movement, window controls, and optionally a toolbar. Edges normally resize. A rare bottom bar is also part of the frame. #### macOS window states An app has one main window; the system has one key/input window at a time. A floating panel can be key while its document stays main. Dock activation brings app windows forward but makes only the recently used one key. Other windows are inactive. Colored close/minimize/zoom controls identify key state; inactive and non-key main windows use gray, and inactive windows lose vibrancy. Some panels take key status only through the title bar or keyboard-input controls. Custom rendering must preserve these automatic state cues. Avoid critical controls at the bottom, which may be offscreen; reserve bottom bars for small contextual summaries, using an inspector for more detail. ### visionOS Windows and volumetric windows can each contain 2D/3D content and coexist in Shared or Full Space. Plain style omits the glass plane. The system positions the first opened surface, then people can move it. #### visionOS windows Default windows use an upright glass plane with close, move, and resize controls, and can add Share, tabs, toolbars, and ornaments. Dynamic scale preserves apparent size across distance. Prefer familiar windows for familiar tasks, reserving immersion for meaningful content. Retain the glass background: it adapts to surroundings and communicates scale and position; removing it weakens legibility and grouping, while an opaque replacement conceals surroundings. Default initial size is 1280×720 pt, placed about 2 meters ahead with an apparent width of about 3 meters. Avoid excess empty space and choose a shape suited to content. Set minimum/maximum sizes and adapt layout throughout. Keep 3D depth shallow in a window because content too far from its surface is clipped; use a volume for deeper objects. #### visionOS volumes Volumes show bounded content from multiple angles; close and move controls turn to face the viewer. Prefer them for rich 3D scenes over UI-centric interfaces. Pin 2D overlays to 3D content with attachments and test multiple viewpoints. Dynamic scaling usually improves distant legibility and interaction, but fixed scaling (the default) suits true-to-life products. From visionOS 2, a baseplate border glow on look reveals bounds and resize controls when content does not fill them. Full-bleed content or a custom baseplate may not need it. Volumes can have an ornament alongside toolbar/tabs: use attachment anchors to keep its position viewer-relative, place it on another edge, and usually add only one. Choose a floor-parallel alignment for largely viewed objects, or a viewer-tilting alignment when interactive content should remain usable while reclining. ## Resources Official implementation links and revision metadata follow. #### Related [Layout](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/layout) [Split views](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/split-views) [Multitasking](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/multitasking) #### Developer documentation — SwiftUI — SwiftUI — UIKit — AppKit #### Videos ## Change log Revision dates recorded by Apple: June 9, 2025, June 10, 2024, June 21, 2023.

# Scroll views Source: [Apple Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/scroll-views) Snapshot: 2026-10-25. Original implementation guidance derived from the source. A scroll view reveals content beyond its bounds through vertical or horizontal movement. The container is visually neutral; transient indicators communicate position and scrolling, with platform-specific behavior. ## Best practices Keep system gestures, keyboard shortcuts, and elastic feedback. Suggest offscreen content with partial items at edges because indicators are not always visible. Avoid nested scrolling on the same axis; orthogonal nested scrolling is acceptable. Page-by-page movement can suit fixed chunks; retain a small overlap, such as a line or part of an image, to preserve context. Automatically reveal hidden relevant content when locating a search result, typing at an offscreen insertion point, extending selection beyond an edge, or acting on a selection after scrolling away. Move only as far as needed; a partially visible selection need not be fully recentered. Bound zoom to useful minimum and maximum scales. ## Scroll edge effects In iOS, iPadOS, and macOS, edge effects separate floating UI from scrolling content beneath. Prefer automatic styling; it provides stronger separation for dense toolbars, uncontained text, or pinned headers. Thoroughly test legibility if choosing soft styling. The hard style gives a more defined opaque boundary; the soft style fades through a variable blur. Use an effect only where floating controls overlap a scroll view, not as decoration or a dark overlay. Apply one per view; split panes can each have one, with aligned heights. ## Platform considerations ### iOS, iPadOS A page control can show position in paged scrolling. Suppress the scroll indicator on that same axis to avoid redundant signals. ### macOS Scroll indicators are also called scroll bars. Small or mini bars can suit tight panels; match other control sizes in that panel. ### tvOS Scrolling follows focus automatically to keep focused content visible, without distinct scroll-view objects and indicators. ### visionOS A small fixed-size indicator stays at the vertical center of the trailing edge or horizontal center of the bottom edge. Swiping reveals it; looking and dragging it enables a jog bar that adjusts scrolling speed rather than absolute position, with tick marks communicating acceleration. Allow adequate margin because this indicator is slightly thicker than on iOS. #### Look to Scroll Eye-only scrolling starts near a scroll boundary and coexists with gestures. Opt in separately for each reading or browsing scroll view; the behavior is not automatic. Avoid it for secondary controls or dense views needing precise quick movement. Apply it consistently across comparable content. Full-width or full-height regions give generous, understandable boundaries; inset regions need clear edges. Remove custom scroll-position effects such as parallax or animation before enabling it to prevent unpredictable behavior. ### watchOS Prefer vertical content that works with the Digital Crown. Use vertical tab views for page-based navigation, with an indicator beside the crown. Keep pages near one screen tall when possible; long pages can scroll and the page indicator expands into a scroll indicator. Use variable heights sparingly and preferably after short fixed pages. ## Resources Official implementation links and revision metadata follow. #### Related [Page controls](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/page-controls) [Gestures](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/gestures) [Pointing devices](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/pointing-devices) #### Developer documentation — SwiftUI — UIKit — AppKit — WatchKit — SwiftUI ## Change log Revision dates recorded by Apple: June 8, 2026, March 24, 2026, July 28, 2025, February 2, 2024, December 5, 2023, June 5, 2023.

# Lists and tables Source: [Apple Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/lists-and-tables) Snapshot: 2026-10-25. Original implementation guidance derived from the source. Lists and tables organize rows into one or more columns, with optional groups, hierarchy, selection, insertion, deletion, and reordering. A navigation list can express an app's structure; a multicolumn table can compare attributes and support sorting. ## Best practices Use rows for text that people need to scan. Consider a collection for many images or highly variable item sizes. Support appropriate editing, including reorder even when addition and removal are unavailable. In iOS and iPadOS, table item selection for editing uses an edit mode. Distinguish selection feedback by purpose: keep a navigation row highlighted to show the current path; for a chosen option, brief row highlighting followed by a persistent checkmark may be more appropriate. ## Content Keep row wording short enough to avoid excessive wrapping or truncation. When items contain lengthy prose, show titles and reveal content in a detail view. Preserve recognizability at narrow widths; middle truncation can retain both ends of an identifying string. Give multicolumn tables descriptive noun or noun-phrase headings in title case without punctuation. If a single-column table has no heading, add context with a label or header. ## Style Choose grouping and row styles that fit the platform and data. iOS and iPadOS grouped lists use headers, footers, and spacing; watchOS elliptical lists visually roll content over a curved surface; macOS bordered tables can use alternating row backgrounds. Use row configurations appropriate to images, text, headers, and footers rather than rebuilding familiar arrangements unnecessarily. ## Platform considerations ### iOS, iPadOS, visionOS An info/detail-disclosure button reveals additional information about a row; a disclosure indicator navigates into the row's hierarchy. Keep these meanings distinct. Avoid placing a section index beside trailing row controls because their targets can interfere with one another. ### macOS Support click-to-sort headings when useful, with another click reversing the sort. Allow column resizing. Alternate row backgrounds can help people track values across wide tables. Use an outline view when the data is hierarchical. ### tvOS Test nearby imagery against the focused row's expansion and rounded corners. Prepare images for those system effects and avoid adding a second corner mask. ### watchOS Favor shorter lists, but preserve access to the full expected dataset. Present relevant items first and offer more rather than silently dropping subscribed or owned items. Vertical page-based movement among row details works only with short detail views; a scrolling detail view prevents swiping directly between detail pages. ## Resources Official implementation links and revision metadata follow. #### Related [Collections](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/collections) [Outline views](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/outline-views) [Layout](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/layout) #### Developer documentation — SwiftUI — SwiftUI — UIKit — AppKit #### Videos ## Change log Revision dates recorded by Apple: June 21, 2023, June 5, 2023.

# Labels Source: [Apple Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/labels) Snapshot: 2026-10-25. Original implementation guidance derived from the source. A label presents short, uneditable text, including an action name, list-item description, or context for nearby controls. SwiftUI provides both Text and Label; component-specific guidance may further constrain the wording. ## Best practices Use a text field for a short editable value and a text view for longer or richly formatted content. Prefer system typography and retain Dynamic Type support where available; check readability whenever introducing custom fonts or styling. Permit selection and copying when the text conveys useful portable information such as an error, address, or location. Use semantic label colors to express hierarchy rather than hard-coded tones: | Role | Typical use | UIKit name | AppKit name | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Primary | Main information | label | labelColor | | Secondary | Supporting text or subheading | secondaryLabel | secondaryLabelColor | | Tertiary | Description of unavailable behavior | tertiaryLabel | tertiaryLabelColor | | Quaternary | Watermark | quaternaryLabel | quaternaryLabelColor | The UIKit column applies to iOS, iPadOS, tvOS, and visionOS. ## Platform considerations No additional iOS, iPadOS, tvOS, or visionOS rules are specified. ### macOS An NSTextField configured as noneditable can display label text. ### watchOS Use system date/time and timer text components for changing temporal information. Date text supports formats, calendars, and time zones; timer text supports count-up and countdown formats. The system adapts presentation to available space and updates values without further app work. These components are also useful in complications. ## Resources Official implementation links and revision metadata follow. #### Related [Text fields](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/text-fields) [Text views](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/text-views) #### Developer documentation — SwiftUI — SwiftUI — UIKit — AppKit ## Change log Revision dates recorded by Apple: June 5, 2023.

Captions describe audible information in synchrony with media, subtitles present dialogue in a chosen language, audio descriptions narrate otherwise visual events in audio pauses, and transcripts provide a complete text account of audible and visual information.
